Pues después de esto me hago un Vladimir y a tomar por culo no? El meme este de los pensamientos más profundos de un hombre heterosexual los tuve yo con 13 años? Pos lo mismo. Lo de que se grabe todo en la misma sala es como curioso??? Pero se cargan esa sensación de aislamiento cuando abren la puerta del jurado para que les manden la prueba y con la escena del baño entonces no sé por que lo han hecho. Con los personajes no me meto mucho por que entiendo que están escritos para que la mayoría no te caiga bien y te toquen los cojones, pero para que los dos mejores personajes sean un señor petulante que no muestra emoción alguna en toda la película y un abuelete que parece que le va a dar un ictus en cualquier momento, los otros os los podéis imaginar. Ya ni hablamos del olor a esmegma que despide esta película con ABSOLUTAMENTE TODO TIOS y la gracia que me ha hecho al final con un plano amplio de la calle desde unas escaleras super altas, ver a una mujer diminuta con un abrigo de piel. En plan para decir que había una mujer en la película. Mi conclusión es que esto no tiene ni pies ni cabeza y que los abogados de ese juicio verdaderamente eran malísimos por que para que los papanatas estos desmontaran el caso, QUE SE PODIA RESOLVER SOLO, EN 20 MINUTOS A LA MÍNIMA QUE LE DIERAS 2 VUELTAS EN LA CABEZA, tenían que haberles regalado el título en la tómbola de la feria; que a lo mejor es por que llevo desde los 9 años viendo CSI y derivados, pero yo desde un primer momento he dicho: todas estas pruebas son circunstanciales y el caso solo tiene sentido si lo miras con estas conjeturas, pero vamos, seré yo que soy muy listo o algo. Y entiendo que me quieren filosofar sobre quienes somos nosotros para decidir quién vive y quien muere, y que en un crimen como este nunca se puede llegar a estar 100% seguro de la verdad al mismo tiempo que me abrían melones de diferencias de clases, prejuicios infundidos injustamente, masculinidades fragiles y de más mariconadas; pero es que no me ha importado tres cojones por que yo desde un principio ya sabía lo que iba a pasar por que era ultra predecible. Mira que no sé, que voy a ver si para compensar mañana me veo Bottoms. Edit: ni 20 minutos después de hacer esta pedazo de review me estoy viendo un broski report y no me avergüenza decir, pensar o confirmar que cualquier cosa que diga esta mujer tiene mayor peso lógico y sociocultural que toda esta película. Mira me vi la película ayer, y lo que veis arriba fue mi reseña pero, es que sinceramente, está es mi cuenta de Lettterboxd y pongo las reseñas que yo quiera y voy a ser completamente transparente con lo que opino sobre esta supuesta obra maestra, ya que no comprendo, porque "tengo que poner una buena reseña", cuando nadie le importan realmente. Primero, partiendo de la base que viendo solo la sinopsis ya me pude imaginar de que iba a ir la película, y lo que lleva de trasfondo (la crítica social), por lo que dice la gente de ella (que es una obra maestra), y sobre todo por el contexto. Primero decir, que entendiendo su contexto me parece que se siga considerando una obra maestra me parece una barbaridad, su guión sinceramente me dio la sensación de ser bastante simple y predecible, no sé si es que he visto películas con grandes plot twist o que, pero es que no me sorprendió lo masss mínimo. A ver, estuve pensando durante toda la película, por lo menos espero que al final, digan quién mato al padre realmente y sea un giro de guión, pero no sé porque me esperaba eso. Ya se que el punto de la película no es desmantelar al asesino, si no la crítica al sistema judicial estadounidense, pero honestamente gente, cuando yo vi que 12 hombres ajenos a todo eso, iba a decidir sobre un joven si iba o no a la silla eléctrica, me pareció cuánto menos una barbaridad, y no me parece nada transgresor lo q los personajes discuten. Me esperaba unas reflexiones más interesantes, profundas sobre la vida y etc. Pero es que es tan superficial. Los "marcos de personaje" son cuanto más aburridos, osea pienso en Wes Anderson y como el lo hace tan bien con los suyos, que al ver una película suya, como the Royal tannebauns, cada uno evoluciona y se nota la función que cumplen y etc. Esto me parece patético, es que es tan obvio lo que cada uno va a responder. Makes sense why this is regarded as one of the best films of all time, so good! Pacing is so good and you jump into the plot right away. For better and worse this movie created a whole legal drama genre that has real life impacts on the justice system. This movie was made 30 years before DNA and I think it’s a stronger movie for the reason that there is no DNA to think about. Juries actually over rely on the presence of DNA (and other iffy Law and Order type science like bullet casing marks) when deliberating a verdict. Get into the nitty gritty! Think about how could one witness hear a scream if the other witness said the train was passing at the exact same moment. This movie is a liberal fantasy that relies on one person insisting on considering the opposing view point, in this case a verdict of not guilty. But, I actually that’s a strength of this movie rather than a weakness. We have to suspend disbelief all the time for a films to be impactful, so why not choose to believe that despite known social and peer pressure someone can voice their disagreement. Devils advocate is usually a negative instigator but it’s fun to watch someone play out that line of argument in a way that is actually worth considering. The justice system is racist. The people making arrests, prosecuting, and deciding criminal cases are racist. The backbone of “justice” should not depend on one good man doing the right thing. Nothing is ever truly objective, which is especially true of the law despite all the language that hopes to make you think it is. I think I’m probably the prime audience for this movie and loved it! I genuinely believe this to be a pillar of not only filmmaking but story telling. The script, is perfect as well as the screenplay. The film tskes place in one room for the majority of its duration, so how do you keep it interesting? You craft the perfect script. Perhaps the most important aspect to really carry the script is the acting. The acting must be independent, each character must be written as though they are the first to be so. 12 Angry Men is built around identity. Each man comes from a unique walk of like with unique experiences and unique opinions. The point of 12 Angry Men is the men coming together. The crux of the story is development, every character changes in some way. The men, despite their unique outlooks, upbringings, and actions must come to a civic and unanimous decision to determine the life of a young man. In order to convey said developments there must be a identity to each character thst is their own entire, and they must be played perfectly for those characterizations. Juror 1, the "leader". He directs the room, but he does not lead it. He is no dictator or supreme leader of thr room, but he has the clipboard, he must declare a vote, he must deliver the decisions. He is not the toughest man in the room, he, more or less, just guides the men. He has his own opinion and he states it clearly. But juror 1 is not stern nor is he Stark. Juror 2, the newbie. Juror 2 has never been on a jury. He doesn't exactly know the directions of debate, but he knows the inner workings of the court. He knows how the court plays and he knows the evidence rather well. He doesn't know how to use his voice clearly over the elders at first, usually being pushed around and silenced. His opinion isn't the clearest either. He says the boy is guilty "just because he is" he's nearly unsure of his own stance, meek in his closed answer. But over time he starts to find his voice. He establishes his knowledge and his eventual confidence. He's inexperienced, coy, and easily pushed around. But he eventually finds himself to reslly prove and get his opinion out. Juror 3, the antithesis. Juror 3 is even labeled by 8 a sadist, which isnt false at all, but his character is deeper than that. He's experienced, older while still having mobility, confidence, and a voice to shout with. He has his definite opinion upon the evidence and he stands by it. He has a solid opinion, he has a genuine belief and he sticks right by it. At his core, he blames the child more than anything. Being a stern father of a son he hasn't seen in two years, he blames the defendant. He knows of his living condition yet he blames the society, he blames the child himself for the possibility of the murder. His pent up rage of his own life pours out in the room, in his opinion. He knows his interpretation of the facts and he knows his opinions, but he is not understanding. He sees his words as the definite truth, he screams and antagonizes and he belittles. He does not work in the view of justice, he works in the view of punishment and of competition, of winning some kind of game of being the 'right one'. Above all else, the man is shadowed by his own life, especially his life with his son, who he in a way blames for their divide. On the same side of the coin, his ultimate anger at the end after he is now the lone juror unleashes and is what ultimately makes him see the error of his ways. He bursts out in an angry monologue. How could anyone, let alone everyone, oppose his definite fact. He takes the photo of his son from his wallet and after seeing what has been the anchor of his rage, rips it to pieces. As soon as he does, he realizes this error, maybe he really is the problem, maybe the boy isn't to blame, maybe it isn't a fact, but it is possible. Juror 4, the statue. Similarly to juror 3, he nearly sees his opinion as fact, but where they differ is approach. Juror 4 knows the evidence well, he knows well upon his own interpretation and opinion, but he is calculated, he is thoughtful in the court system. He does not see this as a game or a competition. He hopes to find whatever Justice he truthfully believes, he is opinionated but he is tolerant in a way. He nearly never sweats and he nearly never moves. As all the men do, he gets angrier as the heat increases and as the temperature rises, but he is clear and concise in his approach. He wants an end, but a right one. He knows his truth but, perhaps begrudgingly, he listens to the other side of the story, and through hearing that he coukd possibly be wrong, he sees the error and realizes that he could possibly be wrong. Juror 5, the experienced. Juror 5 grew up in the same conditions as the defendant. He knows the conditions of the slums, what it can do to a person and how they can operate. Because of his experience, he is particularly sensitive to the prejudices of the other men. He has his beginning opinion but he is nearly embarrassed and certainly unsure of it from the beginning, choosing to pass when asked why he initially votes guilty. He sees the prejudice of the room and he applies his own personal experience with the defendants upbringing and sees that there may be a chance that the boy did not do it. Juror 6, the working man

Por vezes, alguns dos considerados "cânones" do cinema são ainda mais fascinantes do que sua fama tende a sugerir. Assisti 12 Angry Men (1957) com uma noção abstrata prévia, mas realmente não estava esperando que o filme fosse ser tão intrigante e instigante. Não atoa é um filme tão aclamado, é uma obra tão meticulosa em cada um de seus aspectos — sobretudo sua blocagem e encenação — que chega a ser gratificante um filme que se preocupa tanto em trabalhar o cinema numa premissa tão teatral. Ele exemplifica bem, inclusive, a relação que estas duas artes tem. Desde a criação do cinematógrafo, o cinema extraiu muito de sua base no teatro como também em outras artes. Conceitos como mise-en-scène, por exemplo, são emprestados. Mas justamente dessa raiz que a sétima arte se ramificou. No teatro, o olhar vem de amplas perspectivas. Organizar atores, cenários e objetos é um trabalho cuidadoso que oferece um guia em comum a cada pessoa em cada acento. No cinema, essa organização é voltada a um único olhar: o olhar da câmera. Ela permite um close-up em qualquer detalhe que tanto a pessoa da primeira fileira como a última irão observar com perfeita nitidez. Mas também, quando o diretor confia no uso da profundidade de campo em seu filme, ele ganha uma liberdade e oferece um direito ao espectador para olhar o que lhe chama mais atenção no plano — seja no primeiro quanto no segundo plano — .  Num filme de ambiente pequeno e fechado como este, o uso desta ferramenta pode não parecer em primeiro momento, mas é tão relevante quanto o close-up. Quando se há uma visão dos jurados na mesa, o espectador tende a prestar mais atenção naquele que mais lhe gera interesse ou intriga. Conferir por conta própria um pequeno detalhe na interpretação de cada ator na mesa (independente dele ser ou não o principal foco naquele instante). Quando um dos jurados começa a ser abertamente racista e cada um sutilmente se retira da mesa/desvia o olhar/vira as costas, o plano aberto junto a profundidade do campo montam diante de nossos olhos quase que uma pintura. Quando um dos jurados tira a faca do bolso e crava na mesa, a forma como o choque de todos gera desorganização ainda é organizada pela maneira como cada um está presente na imagem de acordo com sua própria expressividade. São inúmeras cenas marcantes. O filme se declara humanista, independente dos fatos. Neste sentido ele é metalinguístico: Independente da verdade, as perspectivas subjetivas são inevitavelmente manipuladas. Votar pela inocência do réu é algo que fere egos, pisa em tabus e preconceitos, indaga convicções, nenhum deles nem o espectador estava na cena do crime. Eles encenam, simulam, deduzem, o cinema é a verdade simulada do mesmo modo. E a indagação que a obra faz segue sendo fundamental sobretudo numa geração tão insensível e  apática quanto a nossa. Cinco minutos é tempo para decidir por uma vida sem pensar em sua realidade, seu contexto, sem se por no lugar? Mais do que a verdade, é isto o que importa para o filme, e para a arte, a única verdade é a de quem reflete a obra.
